p.src: The purpose of the opening recap is not merely to repeat the previous lecture. We need one idea from it in a form that can be carried over to fermions: a mass is a nonzero energy for an excitation at zero momentum. For a field, zero momentum means infinite wavelength, or a displacement that is the same everywhere. A derivative-only theory cannot detect a uniform displacement. A term without derivatives can.

p.src:
Choose the convention $\begin{aligned}
  D_\mu&=\partial_\mu+igA_\mu,
  \\
  \phi&\longmapsto e^{i\theta}\phi,
  \\
  A_\mu&\longmapsto A_\mu-\frac1g\partial_\mu\theta .
\end{aligned}$ The lecture suppresses $g$; keeping it visible makes the dimensions and the eventual mass transparent. Acting on the frozen field gives $\begin{aligned}
  D_\mu\phi
  &=(\partial_\mu+igA_\mu)f e^{i\alpha}
  \notag\\
  &=i\bigl(\partial_\mu\alpha+gA_\mu\bigr)
    f e^{i\alpha}.
  \end{aligned}$ Multiplication by the complex conjugate removes the phase and also turns $i$ times $-i$ into $+1$: $|D_\mu\phi|^2
  =f^2
   \bigl(\partial_\mu\alpha+gA_\mu\bigr)
   \bigl(\partial^\mu\alpha+gA^\mu\bigr).$

en: Parity violation in beta decay

p.src: Begin with the empirical fact that the weak interaction violates parity. Quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics treat a process and its mirror image alike. The weak interaction does not. In neutron beta decay, $n\longrightarrow p+e^-+\bar\nu_e,$ the high-energy electrons selected by the charged-current interaction have left-handed helicity: their spin points opposite to their momentum. The corresponding antineutrinos have the opposite helicity.

The weak interaction couples to a left-chiral electron field and a left-chiral neutrino field, not to a right-chiral electron field in the same way.

p.src:
A Dirac wavefunction has four components. Loosely, two describe spin and two distinguish the positive- and negative-energy solutions, with the latter reinterpreted as antiparticle degrees of freedom. In Hamiltonian form, $i\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial t}
  =\left(-i\bm\alpha\cdot\bm\nabla+m\beta\right)\Psi .$ The matrices $\alpha_i$ and $\beta$ encode the relativistic relation between energy, momentum, and mass.

p.src:
The chiral basis makes the role of $m$ explicit. With $\sigma^\mu=(1,\bm\sigma)$ and $\bar\sigma^\mu=(1,-\bm\sigma)$, $\begin{aligned}
  i\bar\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi_L&=m\psi_R,
  \\
  i\sigma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi_R&=m\psi_L.
  \end{aligned}$ At $m=0$, the equations are independent: a left-chiral field and a right-chiral field can propagate without talking to each other. At $m\neq0$, each appears as the source for the other. This is the exact sense in which a Dirac mass mixes left and right.

p.src:
The corresponding Dirac mass term in the Lagrangian is $\mathcal L_m
  =-m\bar\psi\psi
  =-m\left(\bar\psi_L\psi_R+\bar\psi_R\psi_L\right).$ Under the toy transformation , $\bar\psi_L\psi_R\longmapsto
  e^{-i\theta}\bar\psi_L\psi_R,
  \qquad
  \bar\psi_R\psi_L\longmapsto
  e^{i\theta}\bar\psi_R\psi_L.$ Neither term is invariant. The direct left–right mixing coefficient $m$ is therefore forbidden before symmetry breaking.

p.src: A massive particle can be slowed to rest and accelerated in the opposite direction without reversing its spin. Its helicity then changes sign. A massless particle cannot be overtaken or brought to rest by a Lorentz boost, so its helicity is invariant under proper boosts. This motivates the lecture’s statement that a species with only one physical helicity must be massless. The more exact field-theory statement is that a Lorentz-invariant Dirac mass requires both chiralities.

p.src:
The symmetry forbids a numerical mass, but it allows an interaction with a field that supplies the missing transformation phase. Introduce a complex scalar with $\phi\longmapsto e^{i\theta}\phi,
  \qquad
  \phi^\dagger\longmapsto e^{-i\theta}\phi^\dagger.$ Then $\mathcal L_Y
  =-y\,\bar\psi_L\phi\psi_R
   -y^*\,\bar\psi_R\phi^\dagger\psi_L$ is gauge invariant. In the first term, $\bar\psi_L$ contributes $e^{-i\theta}$ and $\phi$ contributes $e^{i\theta}$; the phases cancel. The second term is its Hermitian conjugate.

p.src:
For the electron, the lecture estimates $y_e\sim\frac{0.5\ \mathrm{MeV}}{10^2\ \mathrm{GeV}}
  \sim10^{-5}.$ Using the canonical value $v=246\ \mathrm{GeV}$ gives the more precise $y_e\simeq2.9\times10^{-6}$. The top quark lies at the opposite end: $y_t=\frac{\sqrt2m_t}{v}\simeq1.$ Thus the Higgs mechanism explains how a gauge-invariant mass can exist, but it does not explain the enormous hierarchy among the $y_i$. The observed fermion masses merely translate that hierarchy into measured numbers.

p.src: There is another logical possibility because the neutrino carries no electric charge. A left-chiral neutrino can be coupled to the charge conjugate of itself, which has the opposite chirality: $\nu_L\longleftrightarrow(\nu_L)^c_R .$ A mass eigenstate built this way is a Majorana fermion: it is its own antiparticle, up to phase conventions. The analogous electron–positron mixing is forbidden because it would violate exact electric-charge conservation.

p.src:
The lecture’s striking summary is that the elementary masses of the minimal Standard Model trace back to one broken vacuum: $\begin{aligned}
  m_W&=\frac12gv,\\
  m_Z&=\frac12\sqrt{g^2+g'^2}\,v,\\
  m_f&=\frac1{\sqrt2}y_fv.
  \end{aligned}$ If $v$ vanished while the dimensionless couplings were held fixed, the weak gauge bosons and charged elementary fermions would be massless.

p.src: This motivates the lecture’s broad naturalness argument. Particles protected by gauge or chiral symmetry remain massless until the Higgs vacuum breaks that protection, so their masses are tied to the relatively small scale $v$. Particles with no such protection may naturally be much heavier and therefore absent from the observed low-energy spectrum. What we see may be a selection effect: the accessible particles are the ones whose masses were forced to wait for electroweak symmetry breaking.

p.src: Mass is not high laboratory energy

p.src:
A cosmic ray strikes a target particle that is approximately at rest. For a projectile proton of laboratory energy $E\gg m_p$, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2
  \simeq2m_pE+2m_p^2,
  \qquad
  \sqrt{s}\simeq\sqrt{2m_pE}.$ Only the square root of the projectile energy becomes center-of-mass energy. For equal head-on beams of energy $E_{\rm beam}$, $\sqrt{s}\simeq2E_{\rm beam}.$ This is why a collider is far more efficient than a fixed target at converting controlled beam energy into new-particle mass.

p.src: The invariant relation $E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4$ contains both meanings. Near rest, $E=mc^2+\frac{p^2}{2m}+\cdots,$ so the same $m$ that gives the rest energy appears in the kinetic response. At high speed the relation between force and acceleration depends on whether the force is parallel or perpendicular to the velocity. This directional dependence is why modern treatments avoid a velocity-dependent relativistic mass and reserve mass for the Lorentz invariant $m$.

p.src: The unifying statement is therefore not that the Higgs is a substance that mechanically drags on particles. It is that the electroweak vacuum has a nonzero scalar order parameter. That order parameter changes which gauge-invariant terms are possible in the low-energy equations. For vectors it opens a zero-momentum gap; for fermions it permits left–right mixing. The different masses then measure different couplings to the same broken vacuum.
